bridges.mechanism: Escalation of kinetic operations generates higher demand for real‑time ISR, imagery analytics, battlefield AI and communications processing, raising short‑term demand for cloud and specialized compute resources.
An uptick in kinetic conflict raises near-term geopolitical risk and the probability of wider disruption, prompting investors to lower risk appetite and reducing aggregate market confidence.
Sustained or intensified conflict compels EU governments to increase defense spending, humanitarian aid and refugee support, directly increasing budgetary commitments and narrowing fiscal space.

A surge in kinetic operations in Ukraine draws US/NATO naval and air assets to the European theatre and stretches intelligence/escort resources, reducing forward deterrence in the Gulf and enabling Iran-backed groups to increase hostile incidents against ships.

A surge in kinetic conflict raises geopolitical and supply‑chain risk premia, prompting risk‑off reallocations and reducing investor confidence in assets and deals tied to US–China tech integration and cross‑border tech exposure.

A deterioration in diesel supply (shortage) raises energy and operational risk for data centers and logistics, reducing project cashflow projections and increasing lender/investor risk premia, thereby raising the effective cost of capital for AI firms.
A tightening diesel supply balance from disrupted imports or redirected flows reduces available refined fuel in markets, directly pushing up diesel and related energy prices across the EU.

A shortfall in Russian diesel exports forces European and other buyers to source refined products from the Middle East, increasing seaborne flows of oil and refined products transiting Gulf routes and chokepoints.

A tightening diesel supply balance constrains inland freight and port-handling capacity, causing delivery delays and lowering the ability of electronics and component supply networks to absorb and reroute disruptions.

Greater government–private operational coordination during the conflict channels rapid procurement, grants and co‑funding to AI firms (for ISR, cybersecurity and logistics), directly increasing the pace of capital deployment into AI projects.

Increased operational coordination and information sharing between governments and private tech companies supplies regulators with transaction-level data and operational support, enabling faster, more targeted implementation and on-the-ground enforcement of tech security and export policies affecting China.

Intensified sanctions and secondary sanctions increase counterparty, correspondent‑bank and asset‑freezing risks, prompting banks and institutional investors to pull or withhold cross‑border capital and reduce allocations to higher‑risk private tech/AI funds.

Escalating and broadened sanctions increase counterparty, compliance and settlement risk for banks and investors, triggering abrupt portfolio rebalancing and cross-border withdrawals that raise capital flow volatility.

Tighter, broader or better-enforced sanctions on Russian oil and petroleum trade reduce available liquidity and alternative supplies in global markets, producing larger and more frequent price swings.

Expansion and stricter enforcement of sanctions during the Russia–Ukraine war creates legal precedent and allied coordination that governments extend to impose broader export controls, licensing restrictions and blacklists on advanced technologies destined for Chinese firms.

A sustained rise in maritime attacks heightens geopolitical risk and prompts cross-border investors and lenders to reprice or withdraw exposure to regional and open-ended technology funds, reducing the pool of deployable capital for AI projects.

An increase in attacks on shipping raises immediate defence, maritime protection and targeted business-support spending and insurance subsidies by EU governments, constraining available fiscal headroom for other policies.

A sustained uptick in Gulf maritime attacks will draw NATO/Western naval and air assets and political attention toward the Middle East, creating openings Russia can exploit to escalate operations in Ukraine or to pressure Kyiv while Western focus and resources are diverted.

A rise in attacks on vessels in the Gulf raises concerns about diversion, theft and dual‑use transfer routes, prompting U.S. regulators and security agencies to broaden or tighten export controls and blacklist authorities to reduce perceived leakages to adversaries.

A reduction in sea-borne oil and refined-product deliveries from Gulf routes (lower maritime_oil_flow) directly tightens physical supply to European refineries and fuel markets, pushing up regional energy prices.

A decline in maritime crude and product flows into key European and regional import hubs directly lowers feedstock availability, forcing refiners to cut throughput and reducing refinery capacity utilization relevant to supplies for the Russia–Ukraine theatre.

Reductions in oil flow through key sea lanes raise near‑term energy and input‑cost risk for manufacturers and cloud/compute operators, generating a more risk‑averse market stance and lowering investor sentiment for tech assets exposed to U.S.–China supply chains.
Spikes in oil-price volatility increase macroeconomic uncertainty and risk premia, widening credit and equity spreads and thereby raising borrowing costs and required returns for AI firms.

Spikes in oil price volatility increase uncertainty about corporate profits, inflation and policy responses, prompting portfolio rebalancing and reducing aggregate investor confidence in European markets.

Marked oil‑price swings increase political and strategic pressure on governments to secure supplies and penalize revenue streams to adversaries, triggering faster and more vigorous enforcement of sanctions, trade screening and export controls by U.S. agencies.

Widespread shipping delays and reroutings raise trade-finance stress and forward-looking earnings uncertainty for exporters/importers, triggering sudden cross-border liquidity moves and larger swings in capital flows into and out of affected EU markets.

Higher levels of shipping disruption (delays, reroutings, insurance-driven cutbacks) reduce seaborne deliveries of diesel and middle distillates into European terminals that supply Ukraine, worsening the diesel supply balance available to Ukrainian forces and civilian markets.

Sustained disruptions that increase transit times, insurance costs and delivery uncertainty make cross‑border M&A and new greenfield investments between U.S. and China less attractive or actionable, causing investors and companies to delay or scale back capital flows dependent on reliable logistics.

Sharper enforcement of tech and security policies raises compliance, licensing and legal risks for AI firms and prompts lenders and investors to demand higher spreads and returns, directly increasing firms' effective cost of capital.

A marked rise in enforcement actions and compliance checks increases regulatory uncertainty and operating costs for EU-headquartered multinationals with US/China exposure, directly reducing investor confidence in EU market stability.

Sharper enforcement (seizures, interdictions and public blacklisting) of tech/sanctions compliance increases confrontations at sea and provokes retaliatory or deterrent strikes by Iran or its proxies against commercial shipping in the Gulf.

A rise in US policy enforcement intensity leads to more aggressive use of secondary sanctions, export-control prosecutions and compliance pressure on intermediaries, directly increasing the effective sanctions pressure applied to Russian actors.

Tighter export controls on high‑end accelerators and related equipment constrain shipments to foreign buyers and induce procurement deferrals, directly lowering short‑term aggregate demand for data‑centre and cloud compute capacity.

Wide-ranging export controls on critical technologies force corporates and funds to abruptly reallocate, cancel deals and pause cross-border projects, generating stop-start investment patterns and spikes in cross-border capital flow volatility.

Targeted export limits on advanced components (e.g., cells, inverters, control electronics) raise procurement and replacement costs for EU renewable and storage projects, tightening supply of low‑cost energy alternatives and putting upward pressure on energy prices.

Broader and tighter export controls force additional vessel inspections, licensing checks, carrier delistings and route changes to avoid interdicted goods, producing immediate delays, reroutings and port bottlenecks in Gulf shipping corridors.

Deterioration in supply‑chain resilience produces component shortages and delivery delays for AI hardware, causing firms to postpone or scale back planned AI capital projects and thereby reducing the near‑term AI investment rate.

Deterioration in market sentiment tied to intensified US–China tech tensions raises risk premia and speculative positioning in energy markets, driving larger and more frequent swings in oil futures and spot prices.

Reductions in cross-border investment flows (eg. blocked foreign VC, curtailed M&A) directly remove pools of external equity and debt available to AI firms in the affected market, shrinking the immediate supply of investable capital.

A sustained fall in inbound US/Chinese direct investment reduces corporate tax receipts, slows investment-driven income and employment growth, and increases deficit financing needs, directly shrinking public fiscal space.

A rapid rise in AI investment, particularly concentrated in a handful of EU member states, draws large, quick cross-border venture, private‑equity and portfolio inflows to those hubs and prompts reallocations and occasional sudden outflows elsewhere, increasing overall capital flow volatility across the bloc.

Faster AI investment accelerates deployment of high‑frequency and news‑sensitive commodity trading algorithms that amplify market reactions to Gulf incidents and signals, increasing short‑term oil price swings.

A faster pace of AI investment expands the number and capability of private AI vendors that governments need for ISR, targeting, logistics and decision‑support, driving more frequent contracting, data‑sharing agreements and integrated operational programs between states and firms.

A sustained surge in AI investment concentrated in one side of the US‑China rivalry (visible via deal volume and fundraising) leads investors to downgrade risk appetite for assets exposed to geopolitical decoupling, lowering overall investor sentiment toward those cross‑border tech exposures.

Higher aggregate demand for compute capacity drives increased data‑centre electricity consumption and fuel purchases (especially in constrained local grids), exerting upward pressure on regional wholesale energy prices.

Rising demand for compute drives expansion of cloud and satellite analytics capacity for near‑real‑time maritime domain awareness, improving detection and interception and thereby deterring or disrupting hostile maritime actions.

Rising demand for high‑end compute (GPUs, HPC, cloud instances) prompts export‑control tightening and targeted enforcement (blocking shipments, restricting cloud access and intermediary suppliers) to prevent advanced compute reaching Russian actors, increasing the scope and rigor of sanctions.

A rapid, observable increase in aggregate compute demand (especially for cutting‑edge GPUs/accelerators) triggers immediate national‑security assessments and political pressure that accelerate and widen export controls on high‑end chips and related tooling.

Sharp growth in compute demand strains capacity for advanced semiconductors, substrates and cooling/packaging inputs, producing bottlenecks and single‑point dependencies that measurably reduce the resilience of international AI hardware supply chains.

An expansion in available investable capital raises private demand for sovereign debt and enables more public‑private financing options, lowering effective sovereign funding costs and thereby widening governments' near‑term fiscal space.

Greater investable capital enables rapid scaling of private AI‑driven convoy protection, autonomous escort services and hardened logistics solutions that reduce rerouting, delays and cargo backlogs during Gulf tensions.

An increase in available investable capital (sovereign, corporate and private) directly funds more outbound M&A, VC and portfolio allocation into foreign AI assets, raising gross and net cross‑border investment flows tied to the tech rivalry.

An increase in cost of capital raises financing costs for Gulf states and commercial actors, delaying or cancelling procurement of AI‑enabled naval defenses and autonomous escorts and reducing deterrence, which makes maritime attacks more likely.

Sharp, AI‑driven spikes in equity valuations that become detached from earnings expectations increase the risk of abrupt corrections and margin stress, which directly undermines aggregate investor confidence in markets.
An increase in prevailing EU policy rates raises bank lending rates and investors' required returns, directly lifting the effective cost of debt and equity that AI firms face when raising finance.
Shrinking fiscal space forces governments to scale back R&D grants, public procurement and co‑investment programs that directly seed and accelerate AI projects, reducing the pace of AI investment.

Increased EU fiscal space enables additional defense and expeditionary funding (naval escorts, allied tasking, sanctions enforcement), directly raising the cost to Iranian actors of maritime interdiction and thereby reducing attack incidence.

Shrinkage of fiscal space forces EU governments to cut or delay defense procurement, joint programs and subsidies, directly reducing the frequency and depth of operational coordination and information-sharing with private defense and logistics firms supporting Ukraine.

Constrained EU fiscal space reduces governments' ability to subsidize strategic sectors, pushing them to prioritize inward investment and short‑term growth incentives by loosening export controls on certain dual‑use tech to attract capital, thereby lowering export restriction levels relevant to the US–China tech contest.

Sustained rises in energy prices increase data‑centre operating costs, prompting cloud providers and large AI users to postpone capacity expansion and throttle nonessential training runs, directly lowering aggregate compute demand.

Acute increases in EU energy prices generate intense domestic political pressure to reduce economic pain, prompting governments to restrict arms shipments or pursue de-escalatory diplomatic steps that lower kinetic operations in the theatre.

Higher energy prices driven by EU cohesion–related disruptions raise production and transport costs for intermediate electronics, causing factory slowdowns and routing frictions that immediately degrade the resilience of tech supply chains contested in the US–China rivalry.

Greater volatility in EU capital flows raises financing and insurance costs for shipowners and commodity traders, prompting route changes, capacity reductions or delays that increase practical disruptions to shipping operations in high‑risk Gulf routes.

Spikes in EU capital‑flow volatility force deal financing interruptions and risk‑off reallocations, directly reducing outbound and inbound cross‑border M&A and portfolio flows tied to US–China tech exposures.

A collapse in EU market confidence precipitates risk-off selling and multiple compression that directly reduces price multiples and private-round valuations applied to AI companies headquartered or listed in the region.

A rise in EU market confidence reduces immediate fiscal and political pressures on capitals, sustaining collective funding and participation in multinational naval patrols and intelligence-sharing that deter Iranian maritime harassment, so higher market confidence tends to lower maritime attack frequency.

A sharp fall in investor confidence heightens political and industry risk aversion within the EU, leading policymakers to scale back new sanctions packages or weaken enforcement to avoid further market dislocation.

A sharp fall in EU market confidence raises perceived geopolitical and economic risk for firms exposed to US–China tech frictions, prompting global investors to mark down and reduce allocations to those assets and thereby lowering overall investor sentiment toward the tech rivalry.

nodes.label: War, Starlink & the Refining Boom: Geopolitics Reshaping Energy and Security
Armed conflict intensity
nodes.description: Measures the aggregate frequency, scale and lethality of kinetic military operations across relevant theatres.

nodes.label: Battlefield communications availability
nodes.description: Measures the operational availability and reliability of tactical communications networks supporting combat operations.

nodes.label: Satellite communications dependency
nodes.description: Measures the degree to which military and critical operations rely on space-based communications and relay services.

nodes.label: Global refining margin level
nodes.description: Measures the average per-barrel profit margin captured across global refining operations for refined fuels.

nodes.label: Refinery capacity utilization
nodes.description: Measures the proportion of installed refining capacity that is actively processing crude into products.

nodes.label: Diesel supply balance
nodes.description: Measures the net flow difference between diesel production/imports and consumption/demand over a rolling period.

nodes.label: Refined product inventories
nodes.description: Measures the aggregate stocks of refined fuels and related products held in commercial and strategic storage.

nodes.label: Energy price volatility
nodes.description: Measures short‑term variability and realized volatility in wholesale oil and refined fuel prices.

nodes.label: Diplomatic cohesion
nodes.description: Measures the degree of policy alignment and coordinated diplomatic action among relevant state coalitions.

nodes.label: State–private coordination intensity
nodes.description: Measures the frequency and depth of operational coordination and information sharing between governments and private sector actors.

nodes.label: Arms transfer rate
nodes.description: Measures the rate and volume of international transfers of weapons, munitions and defense systems into conflict-relevant areas.

nodes.label: Sanctions pressure level
nodes.description: Measures the intensity, scope and enforcement rigor of economic and trade restrictions applied to target actors.

nodes.label: Electronic warfare capability
nodes.description: Measures aggregate capability to conduct electronic, signals and related cyber-interference operations affecting communications and sensors.

nodes.label: Maritime security tension
nodes.description: Measures the level of hostile incidents, interdiction risk and navigational insecurity in strategic sea lanes and coastal zones.

nodes.label: Political polarization in public discourse
nodes.description: Measures the intensity of ideological division and antagonistic framing in public and elite discourse affecting policy options.

nodes.label: Ceasefire probability
nodes.description: Measures the evolving likelihood (as perceived and signalled) of local or broader ceasefires and pauses in hostilities.

Military engagement intensity
nodes.description: The rate and intensity of kinetic military operations and direct strikes among regional actors over time.

nodes.label: Maritime attack frequency
nodes.description: The frequency and tempo of hostile incidents (attacks, mines, drone strikes) targeting vessels and maritime infrastructure.

nodes.label: Maritime oil flow
nodes.description: The volumetric flow of crude oil and refined products transported by sea per unit time along key shipping routes.

nodes.label: Global oil supply–demand balance
nodes.description: The net gap between aggregate oil supply and demand in international markets, measured as excess or deficit volume.

nodes.label: Oil price volatility
nodes.description: The magnitude and frequency of short- and medium-term fluctuations in oil market prices and futures curves.

nodes.label: Market geopolitical risk premium
nodes.description: The additional price component in commodity and asset valuations attributable to perceived geopolitical and security risk.

nodes.label: Shipping disruption level
nodes.description: The degree of interruption to normal commercial shipping operations, measured by delays, reroutings and cargo backlogs.

nodes.label: Diplomatic mediation activity
nodes.description: The tempo and intensity of mediated negotiations, talks and third‑party diplomatic interventions addressing the conflict.

nodes.label: Political and electoral uncertainty
nodes.description: The level of uncertainty in domestic political outcomes and decisionmaking that affects policy signaling and strategic choices.

nodes.label: Proxy actor operational activity
nodes.description: The rate of operations, strikes and logistical actions undertaken by non‑state or proxy forces linked to principal belligerents.

nodes.label: Blockade and chokepoint extent
nodes.description: The spatial scope and severity of blockades, interdictions and chokepoint congestion affecting maritime and overland trade corridors.

nodes.label: Corporate liquidity and cash buffers
nodes.description: The aggregate level of cash and readily available liquid assets held by energy-sector firms to absorb revenue and operational shocks.

nodes.label: Government reserve stock level
nodes.description: The aggregated volume of government-held liquid fuel reserves available for emergency release to stabilise markets.

nodes.label: Shipping insurance premia
nodes.description: The level of insurance loadings and war-risk premia charged for maritime carriage of energy cargoes through contested areas.

nodes.label: Port capacity utilization
nodes.description: The degree to which ports, terminals and transshipment hubs are operating relative to their usual throughput capacity.

nodes.label: Financial market volatility
nodes.description: The pace and amplitude of volatility in financial markets (equities, credit spreads, FX and macro rates) in response to geopolitical shocks.

nodes.label: U.S. military options and decision window on Iran
Continued strikes and mine incidents in Strait of Hormuz and regional waters
China's economic-political pivot reshaping global markets and industries
Political control level
nodes.description: Degree of centralized political tightening and internal discipline within governing structures, measured as the intensity and scope of top-down political directives and internal purges.

nodes.label: Policy enforcement intensity
nodes.description: Rate and vigor with which new and existing policies (regulatory, export or security) are implemented and enforced across economic and administrative channels.

nodes.label: Export restriction level
nodes.description: Stringency and breadth of controls limiting cross-border transfer of goods, technologies and services, including licensing, blacklists and practical barriers.

nodes.label: Advanced technology accessibility
nodes.description: Degree to which advanced technologies (designs, equipment, know‑how) are available to domestic and foreign firms through trade, licensing and supply arrangements.

nodes.label: Domestic demand growth rate
nodes.description: Rate of change in internal consumer and business demand for goods and services within the domestic economy.

nodes.label: Industrial capacity utilization
nodes.description: Proportion of productive industrial capacity currently in use relative to potential maximum output across key manufacturing sectors.

nodes.label: Global supply chain resilience
nodes.description: System-wide ability of international supply networks to absorb disruptions, re-route inputs and maintain delivery of critical components.

nodes.label: Multinational market accessibility
nodes.description: Ease with which foreign-affiliated firms can enter, operate and sell in the domestic market, including licensing, joint-venture barriers and informal constraints.

nodes.label: Corporate earnings surprise rate
nodes.description: Frequency and magnitude of firms' reported earnings deviating from market expectations over time.

nodes.label: Investor sentiment
nodes.description: Aggregate market perception of risk and return prospects for assets exposed to the system, reflecting confidence, fear and forward-looking expectations.

nodes.label: Capital market volatility level
nodes.description: Degree of price variability and risk premia in equity, bond and currency markets influenced by system shocks and uncertainty.

nodes.label: Cross-border investment flows
nodes.description: Net and gross movements of capital across borders for direct investment, portfolio allocation and M&A activity.

nodes.label: Regulatory policy activity rate
nodes.description: Pace at which new rules, guidance and formal regulatory changes are issued by authorities and relevant regulators.

nodes.label: Geopolitical incident frequency
nodes.description: Rate at which regional political or security incidents occur that affect cross-border trade, navigation or diplomatic relations.

nodes.label: Public backlash intensity
nodes.description: Level of social, consumer and media-driven backlash against firms, cultural products or foreign actors, measured by protests, boycotts and social-media amplification.

nodes.label: Corporate strategy reorientation rate
nodes.description: Speed at which firms alter supply chains, investment plans, product strategies and market allocations in response to evolving policy and market signals.

Increased PLA naval activity near Taiwan

AI investment rate
nodes.description: Pace at which new capital is being allocated to AI-related projects, infrastructure and teams per unit time.

nodes.label: Compute capacity demand
nodes.description: Aggregate demand for data‑centre and cloud compute resources expressed as required compute units or utilization levels.

nodes.label: Capital availability
nodes.description: Overall supply of investable capital accessible to AI projects and firms across equity, debt and private markets.

nodes.label: Cost of capital
nodes.description: Effective price (interest rates, required returns, yield spreads) firms face when raising debt or equity funding.

nodes.label: Corporate cash reserves
nodes.description: Aggregate liquid cash and near‑cash holdings available within firms to fund operations and investment in AI.

nodes.label: Profitability margins
nodes.description: Average operating and net margin levels across firms engaged in AI build‑out, reflecting profitability per unit revenue.

nodes.label: Operating cost pressure
nodes.description: Rate of upward pressure on recurring costs (compute, staffing, facilities, energy) experienced by firms.

nodes.label: Investor risk appetite
nodes.description: Aggregate willingness of investors to accept funding risk, long time horizons and valuation uncertainty in AI ventures.

nodes.label: Equity valuation levels
nodes.description: Typical market price multiples and capitalization levels applied to firms involved in AI across public and private markets.

nodes.label: Fundraising flow volume
nodes.description: Total rate and dollar volume of capital being raised for AI activity through IPOs, equity offerings and private rounds.

nodes.label: Debt issuance flow
nodes.description: Rate and volume of new debt being issued to finance AI investments, including bonds and bank lending.

nodes.label: Talent supply
nodes.description: Available pool of skilled workers (engineering, research, ops) able to be employed in AI development and deployment.

nodes.label: Layoffs and buyouts rate
nodes.description: Frequency and scale of workforce reductions, voluntary buyouts and rehiring flows affecting AI and adjacent teams.

nodes.label: Regulatory scrutiny intensity
nodes.description: Level of policy and regulatory attention, enforcement activity and compliance requirements directed at AI activities.

nodes.label: Energy and commodity constraints
nodes.description: Availability, price pressure and physical limits in energy and key commodities (power, metals) needed for AI infrastructure.

nodes.label: Market volatility
nodes.description: Degree of short‑term price volatility and sentiment swings in financial markets that affect valuations and funding access.

nodes.label: Post‑IPO credit rating decision for Anthropic
Big tech delays or flattens capex
Rising regulation and scrutiny of AI agents
Microsoft voluntary buyouts and workforce reshaping
Copper and commodity constraints check AI build‑out
Europe’s economic-political stress: ECB transition, energy shock, fiscal strain
Monetary policy uncertainty
nodes.description: Degree of unpredictability in central bank decision-making and leadership stability affecting expectations about future policy actions.

nodes.label: Policy interest rate level
nodes.description: Prevailing short-term policy interest rate that sets the baseline cost of borrowing across the economy.

nodes.label: Sovereign bond market volatility
nodes.description: Magnitude and frequency of yield and price fluctuations in sovereign debt markets.

nodes.label: Fiscal space
nodes.description: Degree to which public finances can be adjusted (spending increases or tax cuts) without triggering adverse market responses.

nodes.label: Energy price level
nodes.description: Market price level of key energy commodities that influences production costs and consumer expenditures.

nodes.label: Energy supply risk
nodes.description: Probability and expected severity of disruptions to energy production, transport or availability.

nodes.label: Capital flow volatility
nodes.description: Variability and incidence of cross-border capital inflows and outflows that affect local financing conditions.

nodes.label: Market confidence
nodes.description: Aggregate investor belief in financial market stability and future returns that conditions risk-taking and pricing.

nodes.label: Banking sector liquidity
nodes.description: Availability of liquid assets within the banking system to support lending, intermediation and withdrawal demands.

nodes.label: Credit spread level
nodes.description: Average premium over risk-free rates required by lenders for bearing credit risk across non-sovereign borrowers.

nodes.label: Private credit supply
nodes.description: Flow of lending capacity and willingness from non-bank financial intermediaries and private lenders into the economy.

nodes.label: Real estate valuation pressure
nodes.description: Rate and direction of deviation in property prices relative to underlying economic fundamentals, indicating overheating or distress.

nodes.label: Political cohesion strength
nodes.description: Degree of alignment and cooperative functioning among political actors and jurisdictions influencing policy coordination.

nodes.label: Electoral political risk
nodes.description: Perceived probability and likely impact of electoral outcomes that materially change policy direction or stability.

nodes.label: Inflation expectations
nodes.description: Anticipated future inflation by households, firms and markets that informs wage-setting, pricing and policy responses.

nodes.label: Policy signalling credibility
nodes.description: Degree to which official communications and signals about future policy are judged believable and likely to be implemented.

A sustained surge in AI investment concentrated in one side of the US‑China rivalry (visible via deal volume and fundraising) leads investors to downgrade risk appetite for assets exposed to geopolitical decoupling, lowering overall investor sentiment toward those cross‑border tech exposures.

Sharp growth in compute demand strains capacity for advanced semiconductors, substrates and cooling/packaging inputs, producing bottlenecks and single‑point dependencies that measurably reduce the resilience of international AI hardware supply chains.

Spikes in EU capital‑flow volatility force deal financing interruptions and risk‑off reallocations, directly reducing outbound and inbound cross‑border M&A and portfolio flows tied to US–China tech exposures.

A sharp fall in EU market confidence raises perceived geopolitical and economic risk for firms exposed to US–China tech frictions, prompting global investors to mark down and reduce allocations to those assets and thereby lowering overall investor sentiment toward the tech rivalry.
